original_question: Fix an integer k >= 4. Beyond the known polygonal examples, are there other k-reflective projective billiards in classes of domains with prescribed boundary regularity such as polygonal, piecewise-algebraic, or analytic boundaries?
target_in_paper: Corentin Fierobe, Problem 1, Question 2, titled “Projective Ivrii’s conjecture.” ([armj.math.stonybrook.edu](https://armj.math.stonybrook.edu/pdf-Springer-final/022-0198.pdf))
correct_elements: Your draft already captures the right target very closely: it keeps the paper’s range k ≥ 4, asks for other examples of k-reflective projective billiards beyond the currently known polygonal ones, and uses the same sample boundary classes named in the paper (polygonal, piecewise-algebraic, analytic). ([armj.math.stonybrook.edu](https://armj.math.stonybrook.edu/pdf-Springer-final/022-0198.pdf))
missing_details: The ambient setting should be stated explicitly: the paper is about projective billiards in the Euclidean plane, not in higher dimensions or in an abstract projective-geometric setting. ([armj.math.stonybrook.edu](https://armj.math.stonybrook.edu/pdf-Springer-final/022-0198.pdf))

A projective billiard is not just a domain: it is a bounded domain Ω ⊂ R² with a (piecewise) smooth boundary ∂Ω endowed with a smooth transverse line field L. ([armj.math.stonybrook.edu](https://armj.math.stonybrook.edu/pdf-Springer-final/022-0198.pdf))

The reflection law should be specified: if an oriented line ℓ meets ∂Ω at p, its reflection ℓ′ is defined by requiring that ℓ, ℓ′, L(p), and T_p∂Ω form a harmonic quadruple. ([armj.math.stonybrook.edu](https://armj.math.stonybrook.edu/pdf-Springer-final/022-0198.pdf))

The surrounding context also notes that ordinary billiards are included as the special case when L(p) is orthogonal to ∂Ω. ([armj.math.stonybrook.edu](https://armj.math.stonybrook.edu/pdf-Springer-final/022-0198.pdf))

To make the question stand-alone, the paper’s meaning of “k-reflective” should be included: the associated billiard map has an open set of periodic points. ([armj.math.stonybrook.edu](https://armj.math.stonybrook.edu/pdf-Springer-final/022-0198.pdf))

The known-example context should be recorded accurately: the paper says examples are known for k = 3 and for every even k ≥ 4, and all these known examples are projective billiards inside polygons. ([armj.math.stonybrook.edu](https://armj.math.stonybrook.edu/pdf-Springer-final/022-0198.pdf))

It is also useful to note that the separate preceding question is about the existence of examples with k ≥ 5 odd; your draft correctly targets the broader Question 2 rather than that odd-k-only Question 1. ([armj.math.stonybrook.edu](https://armj.math.stonybrook.edu/pdf-Springer-final/022-0198.pdf))

The official formulation is existential within a chosen regularity class (“within a class of domains with a specific boundary smoothness”), so the refined question should preserve that per-class scope rather than broaden into a global classification problem over all regularities at once. ([armj.math.stonybrook.edu](https://armj.math.stonybrook.edu/pdf-Springer-final/022-0198.pdf))
refined_question: Let Ω ⊂ R² be a bounded planar domain whose (piecewise) smooth boundary ∂Ω is endowed with a smooth transverse line field L, and let the projective billiard reflection law be defined by the requirement that at each impact point p ∈ ∂Ω the incoming line ℓ, the reflected line ℓ′, the transverse line L(p), and the tangent line T_p∂Ω form a harmonic quadruple. Given an integer k ≥ 4, are there, within a prescribed class of boundary smoothness (for example polygonal, piecewise-algebraic, or analytic), any examples of k-reflective projective billiards other than the known polygonal ones, where “k-reflective” is understood in the paper’s sense that the associated billiard map has an open set of periodic points? ([armj.math.stonybrook.edu](https://armj.math.stonybrook.edu/pdf-Springer-final/022-0198.pdf))
justification: The draft is clearly aiming at Corentin Fierobe’s Projective Ivrii’s conjecture, namely Problem 1, Question 2, because it keeps the same lower bound k ≥ 4 and asks for other k-reflective projective billiards under boundary-regularity restrictions. The surrounding paragraph on the same page supplies exactly the hidden assumptions needed for a stand-alone formulation: what a planar projective billiard is, how the harmonic reflection law is defined, what “k-reflective” means in the paper, and which polygonal examples are already known. ([armj.math.stonybrook.edu](https://armj.math.stonybrook.edu/pdf-Springer-final/022-0198.pdf))
